topic: Greenland shark longevity measured by eye-lens radiocarbon dating
title: This Shark Was Born Before the Steam Engine
target_audience: 18-40, curious international viewers of science shorts

visual.style: Dark underwater documentary, single warm light source per shot, film grain.

scenes.text: There's a shark in the Arctic... that is probably older than the United States.
scenes.visual_goal: Hook: a silhouette glides into the single warm shaft of light under the ice.

scenes.text: It's called the Greenland shark. It lives in water close to freezing...
scenes.visual_goal: Side profile tracking shot, rim light from above.

scenes.text: and moves slower than you walk.
scenes.visual_goal: Vast ice ceiling; the shark small, nearly still: slowness and cold.

scenes.text: For decades, no one could tell its age. Sharks don't have the bones scientists usually count.
scenes.visual_goal: Dark lab table, desk lamp: tally marks crossed out (no bones to count).

scenes.text: So in twenty sixteen, researchers looked into its eyes.
scenes.visual_goal: Push-in on the clouded eye with its parasite.

scenes.text: The core of the eye lens forms before birth, and never changes. Carbon dating it gave an answer.
scenes.visual_goal: Inside the lens: glass layers form outward from a glowing core.

scenes.text: The largest shark they studied was around four hundred years old. Give or take a century.
scenes.visual_goal: Split cutaway: centuries pass above (ships, skies), the shark barely moves below.

scenes.text: And it doesn't become an adult until it's about one hundred and fifty.
scenes.visual_goal: Close pass of the ancient, scarred head.

scenes.text: So the oldest ones down there were young before the steam engine... and they're still in no hurry.
scenes.visual_goal: The shark sinks away; the light collapses into the ODDLIGHT dot.

sources.citation: Nielsen J. et al. (2016) Eye lens radiocarbon reveals centuries of longevity in the Greenland shark (Somniosus microcephalus). Science 353(6300):702-704
Watanabe Y.Y., Lydersen C., Fisk A.T., Kovacs K.M. (2012) The slowest fish: swim speed and tail-beat frequency of Greenland sharks. J. Exp. Mar. Biol. Ecol. 426-427:5-11
Encyclopaedia Britannica, "Newcomen engine" (first practical steam engine, 1712)

claims.text: The oldest Greenland sharks are probably older than the United States (1776): minimum lifespan 272 years.
Greenland sharks live in near-freezing Arctic/North Atlantic water.
They cruise at ~0.34 m/s (~1.2 km/h), slower than human walking pace.
Sharks lack the calcified bony structures normally used for age counting, so their age was long unknown.
In 2016 researchers radiocarbon-dated the eye lens nuclei of Greenland sharks.
The eye lens nucleus forms before birth and is metabolically inert, so it can be radiocarbon dated.
The largest shark studied (502 cm) was estimated at 392 ± 120 years.
Sexual maturity is reached at roughly 156 ± 22 years.
A ~400-year-old shark (born c. 1620) would have been young (pre-maturity) when the first practical steam engine appeared (1712).
claims.note: Narration hedges: 'the oldest ones ... were young before the steam engine'.
